### Higher-Moment Instruments for Measurement Error {#sec-higher-moment-iv}

The investment literature has a measurement problem so severe that it generated its own estimator.
Theory says investment responds to marginal $q$, the shadow value of an additional unit of
capital. What the data contain is average $q$, a ratio of market value to book value that
measures marginal $q$ with enormous error. Ordinary least squares of investment on average $q$ is
attenuated, and the standard reading, that investment is insensitive to fundamentals and
therefore driven by cash flow and financial constraints, may be an artifact of that attenuation.

@erickson2000measurement showed how to identify the coefficient without an external instrument,
using the higher moments of the mismeasured regressor. It belongs beside the copula correction of
Section \@ref(sec-copula-correction) and Lewbel's construction of
Section \@ref(sec-lewbel-heteroskedasticity): all three buy identification with a distributional
assumption rather than with outside variation.

#### Where the Identification Comes From

Take the classical errors-in-variables model, centred for convenience:

$$
y_i = \beta x_i^* + u_i, \qquad x_i = x_i^* + e_i,
$$

with $x^*$, $u$, and $e$ mutually independent and mean zero. Least squares is attenuated by the
familiar reliability ratio. Second moments alone cannot separate $\operatorname{Var}(x^*)$ from
$\operatorname{Var}(e)$, which is why the model is not identified from the covariance matrix.

Third moments can, provided the true regressor is skewed. Taking expectations,

$$
\mathbb{E}[y x^2] = \beta\, \mathbb{E}[x^{*3}], \qquad
\mathbb{E}[x^3] = \mathbb{E}[x^{*3}] + \mathbb{E}[e^3],
$$

so if the measurement error is symmetric, $\mathbb{E}[e^3] = 0$, and

$$
\hat\beta = \frac{\widehat{\mathbb{E}}[y x^2]}{\widehat{\mathbb{E}}[x^3]}.
$$

The estimator needs $\mathbb{E}[x^{*3}] \neq 0$. If the true regressor is symmetric the
denominator is zero in population and the estimator has no content, which is the same structural
warning that attaches to the copula method: the identifying feature is a departure from
symmetry, and when the data are close to symmetric the estimator is near-singular rather than
merely imprecise.

@erickson2002two develop the general case as a GMM problem using moments of order three and
higher, with covariates partialled out, which is what applied work in finance actually uses.

#### Demonstration

```{r hmiv-demo, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
set.seed(303)

ew <- function(n = 5000, skew = TRUE) {
  # True regressor: right-skewed when skew = TRUE, symmetric otherwise.
  xstar <- if (skew) (rchisq(n, 3) - 3) / sqrt(6) else rnorm(n)
  e <- rnorm(n)            # symmetric measurement error: E[e^3] = 0
  u <- rnorm(n)
  beta <- 1.0
  y <- beta * xstar + u
  x <- xstar + e           # what the analyst observes

  yc <- y - mean(y); xc <- x - mean(x)
  c(OLS = unname(coef(lm(y ~ x))[2]),
    third_moment = mean(yc * xc^2) / mean(xc^3),
    skewness_of_x = mean(xc^3) / sd(x)^3)
}

out <- t(sapply(c(TRUE, FALSE), function(s)
  c(skewed_regressor = s, round(rowMeans(replicate(200, ew(skew = s))), 3))))
knitr::kable(out, row.names = FALSE,
  caption = paste("Third-moment estimator for the classical errors-in-variables",
                  "model. True coefficient is 1.0. Identification requires the",
                  "true regressor to be skewed."))
```

With a skewed true regressor, least squares is attenuated to about one half of the truth while
the third-moment estimator recovers 1.0 almost exactly. With a symmetric regressor the
denominator is estimating zero, and the estimator returns noise. Nothing in the output flags
this: there is no first-stage statistic to inspect, so the sample skewness of the observed
regressor is the diagnostic, and it has to be reported.

#### What This Does and Does Not Buy

The estimator addresses measurement error, and only measurement error. It assumes the regression
error $u$ is independent of the true regressor, which rules out the simultaneity and omitted
variables that motivate most instrumental variables work. Applied to an endogeneity problem that
is not an errors-in-variables problem it will return a number, and the number will be wrong.

That distinction matters for how the finance results should be read. Using these estimators,
@erickson2000measurement find that investment is far more responsive to $q$ than least squares
suggests, and that the apparent explanatory power of cash flow largely disappears. That is a
claim about measurement, not about whether firms face financing frictions, and it stands or falls
on whether average $q$ really does measure marginal $q$ with classical error.

Three assumptions carry the result and none is testable from the estimation sample:

1.  Measurement error is symmetric. Skewed measurement error contaminates the denominator
    directly, since $\mathbb{E}[x^3]$ then mixes $\mathbb{E}[x^{*3}]$ with $\mathbb{E}[e^3]$.
2.  Measurement error is independent of the true regressor, not merely uncorrelated. Independence
    is what licenses the higher-moment restrictions, and it is much stronger than what classical
    errors-in-variables needs at second order.
3.  The structural error is independent of the true regressor, which is the assumption that
    confines the method to measurement error.

#### Practice

1.  Report the skewness of the mismeasured regressor and treat weak skewness the way you would
    treat a weak first stage.
2.  Report estimates using third moments and higher moments separately. Instability across moment
    orders is evidence that the distributional assumptions are doing more work than the data
    support.
3.  Show the least squares estimate alongside, and state the implied reliability ratio. If it
    implies that the observed regressor is almost all noise, that is a substantive claim about the
    measure that a reader should be able to evaluate.
4.  Where an external instrument exists, report both. Agreement is real evidence; disagreement
    tells you the measurement-error model is not the whole story.
